title: Scaling real-time connections
description: Project: Scaling real-time connections. Build and understand this project with step-by-step guidance.

data.text: A single server can hold a few thousand WebSocket connections, but real-world products need tens or hundreds of thousands. Scaling real-time connections requires understanding the bottlenecks in memory, CPU, network file descriptors, and the message bus that connects server instances. This lesson covers the patterns that let you grow horizontally without losing the low-latency guarantees users expect.

items: Connection capacity per server depends on available file descriptors and memory per connection
Stateless application servers let you add instances behind a load balancer without session affinity
Pub/sub message bus decouples connection managers from message routing
Room-based broadcasting minimizes unnecessary network traffic
Horizontal scaling requires consistent routing: which server holds which connection?
Capacity planning: measure current usage, identify the bottleneck, then scale the constrained resource
Autoscaling with real-time connections requires careful warm-up and drain policies

terms.definition: An operating system handle for an open file, socket, or pipe. Each WebSocket connection consumes one file descriptor.
A messaging pattern where publishers send messages to channels and subscribers receive messages from channels they have joined, without knowing about each other.
A load balancer routing strategy that sends all requests from a client to the same server instance, used when server-side state exists.
Adding more server instances to distribute load, as opposed to vertical scaling which adds more resources to a single server.
A process that stops accepting new connections on a server instance and waits for existing connections to close before removing it from the pool.

data.text: Without a scaling strategy, the first popular feature can exhaust connection limits and crash the server. Scaling real-time systems is not just about adding more machines; it is about choosing the right architecture so that each added machine contributes useful capacity. A pub/sub design with stateless connection managers scales linearly, while a stateful design with sticky sessions requires complex failover and rebalancing.

data.title: Know your bottleneck
data.text: Use operating system tools like ss, netstat, and lsof to measure file descriptor usage. Use top and vmstat to measure CPU and memory. Do not scale horizontally until you know which resource is constrained; adding servers to a CPU-bound system does not help if the bottleneck is disk I/O.

items: Increase file descriptor limits: raise ulimit -n to one hundred thousand or more on Linux
Tune TCP parameters: enable tcp_tw_reuse and reduce tcp_fin_timeout to reclaim sockets faster
Use an external message bus like Redis, NATS, or Kafka to route messages between connection manager instances
Group connections into rooms and broadcast only to the room members served by each instance
Place a reverse proxy like NGINX or HAProxy in front to terminate TLS and distribute WebSocket upgrades
Implement autoscaling with warm-up: new instances should not receive traffic until they have joined the message bus

data.text: Comparison: stateful versus stateless connection managers

cards.title: Stateful with sticky sessions
cards.description: Each server instance stores connection state and the load balancer routes a user to the same instance.
pros: No message bus required for same-server messages

cards.title: Stateless with pub/sub
cards.description: Server instances are interchangeable; a message bus routes messages to the instance holding a given connection.
cons: Message bus is a new dependency
Slightly higher latency for cross-instance messages

data.title: Capacity plan a real-time service
data.description: Given the following targets, design a capacity plan: ten thousand concurrent WebSocket connections per server, fifty messages per second per room, one hundred rooms per server instance. Calculate the total servers needed for one million concurrent users and five hundred thousand messages per second across all rooms.
steps: Calculate file descriptors and memory per connection
Determine how many connections each server instance can hold
Calculate the number of server instances required for one million concurrent users
Identify the bottleneck and describe how you would test it before production
data.expectedOutcome: You should produce a capacity model with clear assumptions and a plan for load testing each bottleneck.

data.title: Summary
points: Stateless connection managers with pub/sub scale linearly
Increase file descriptor limits before adding servers
Use rooms to minimize unnecessary broadcast traffic
Warm up new instances before sending live traffic
data.takeaway: Scaling real-time systems is about removing state from individual servers and distributing work through a shared message bus.
